02 — RESEARCH

Research Projects

Undergraduate Research under the Grainger College of Engineering

Magnetorquer-Based Control Simulation Using FreeFlyer

Magnetorquers are the primary actuator LEO spacecraft use to dump excess momentum from saturated reaction wheels and they generate a control torque by pushing a magnetic dipole against Earth's magnetic field. This project built a FreeFlyer simulation of the MonARCH CubeSat to size the magnetorquer needed to keep its three reaction wheels within their operating limits over a full year in a 550 km orbit.

The simulation applies a B-dot control law for momentum dumping and accounts for solar radiation pressure and aerodynamic drag torques from a six-plate spacecraft model. An uncapped dipole moment against a 0.1 A·m² limit showed that capping the dipole moment allows for fewer, higher-peak activations (up to 3.5 A·m²) for smaller, more frequent, and more hardware-realistic corrections for the mission's Preliminary Design Review.

Surface Evolution Modeling from Experimental Plume–Surface Interactions

When the rocket's exhaust hits the ground during landing, the exhaust carves out a crater that is a source of uncertainty for hardware and terrain. Using 2D crater profiles from NASA, this project fits the crater through Bézier surfaces to demonstrate how craters evolve over time.

Two strategies were compared with aligning initial control points vertically to the nearest contour by depth versus projecting them along the surface normal or perpendicular projection. The depth-aligned approach converged more smoothly and reliably, and tuning the cost function's smoothing-penalty weight further reduced fitting error across test cases. These are the initial steps to building a model that can predict how new craters will form and evolve during planetary landings.
